title: Title II PDF Backlog Index: US Counties of 50,000+ | SignalFeed.dev
description: Automated measurements of PDF accessibility on the websites of 426 US counties facing the April 26, 2027 ADA Title II compliance date: untagged and scanned PDFs, veraPDF results and estimated pages to remediate.
h1: Title II PDF Backlog Index: US counties of 50,000+
body:
On April 26, 2027, every US county with 50,000 or more residents (in the most recent decennial Census) reaches its compliance date under the ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR part 35, subpart H): web content, including PDFs, must conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, subject to the rule's exceptions. We measured what that means for the documents these counties actually publish: agendas, budgets, plans, forms and notices. For the same measurement of cities, see the city Backlog Index.

What we found

  • 426 of 871 counties measured (the rest blocked automated visitors, host their documents elsewhere, or had too few PDFs to sample; they are reported as "insufficient sample", never as clean).
  • 19,831 PDFs analyzed. 45.1% were untagged, which means a screen reader gets no structure at all, and 19.7% were scanned, image-only pages with no usable text.
  • 10 of 1276 sampled PDFs passed the veraPDF PDF/UA-1 checks.
  • New documents too: of 8,519 sampled PDFs last modified in 2025 or 2026, 32.7% were untagged. Setting up accessible export now helps keep the backlog from growing.
  • The median measured county has roughly 1,909 pages of PDFs failing at least one basic check (untagged, no document language, or scanned). Across all measured counties that is on the order of 3,800,000 pages. This is a sample-based estimate, and a few very long documents can inflate an individual county's number.

What this is, and what it isn't

These are automated signals, not a conformance evaluation. An automated check can show that a PDF definitely fails (for example, it has no tags). It can never show that a PDF conforms: that takes human review, including with assistive technology. Treat the numbers as the size of the problem, not as a verdict on any county.

Not every PDF has to be fixed. The rule has exceptions for archived web content and for preexisting conventional electronic documents, unless they are currently used to apply for, access or participate in a service. We record how recently each document was modified so that this can be judged; the estimates above do not subtract exempt documents.

Method

  • Targets: US counties with 50,000+ residents that have an official website listed in Wikidata (871 counties). Consolidated city-counties already in the city index are left out.
  • Crawler: obeys robots.txt and crawl delays, makes at most one request per second per site, identifies itself honestly, never logs in, and stops at any bot challenge. It reads up to 150 pages and the site's sitemaps, then samples up to 60 PDFs per county.
  • Checks per PDF: tags (structure tree), document language, title, scanned/image-only pages, page count and modification date. A small sample per county also gets veraPDF PDF/UA-1 validation.
  • Estimated pages are scaled from the sample to all PDF links found on the pages we could reach. Counties that keep documents on separate systems (court, land-records or agenda portals) are undercounted.
  • Data as of 2026-11-20. We don't collect personal information; contact emails are not stored.

Get the per-county data

The workbook lists every targeted county (measured or not): PDFs found and estimated, untagged and scanned shares, recent-document share, estimated pages needing remediation, a rough market size, and the days left to the compliance date. It's built for remediation firms, consultants and web agencies deciding where to focus, and for agencies benchmarking against their peers.
